A guide to power in Africa · October 2026

Africa Power Architecture & Stack

The Africa Power Stack is a map of how political power works across much of the continent: who holds it, how money, force, votes and approval move between them, and why long-serving leaders are so hard to replace. It is called a stack because power is layered, from foreign powers and lenders at the top, through the inner circle around the ruler, down to challengers and ordinary people at the bottom.

The central tension. Throughout this guide, notice one tension: what maximizes public welfare, opportunity and quality of life for all Africans is often different from what keeps the system stable for those who gain from it. Almost every role faces daily choices between the two.

If you plan to build a career in Africa, or deal with the continent in any way, as a worker, investor, student, creator or visitor, this guide will help you understand your role, even a small one, in reinforcing or changing the system.

How to use this guide
  1. Understand the system. Parts 1 to 7 explain how the system was built and who it serves, the map of players, its weak points, why it resists change, the paths to change, what works, and the warning signs.
  2. Find yourself in it. Part 8 lets you choose from 74 careers and voter types and see where you sit, what you earn, how your vote counts, your risks, and the choices you face.
  3. Compare. Part 9 shows how pay and closeness to power go together across all careers.
  4. Ask. Part 10 answers common questions, such as why free trade and free movement are so hard in Africa.

Prefer to listen? In Part 8, press Listen to Angwi for any career. For the map on its own, open the Africa Power Stack.

Part 1 · How the system was built, and who it serves

Who built the Power Stack?

No single person, country or era designed it. The Power Stack was built in layers over centuries, and especially over the last 140 years, by many actors with very different amounts of power. Colonial rule and what followed it shaped the system more than anything else: borders, economies built to export raw materials, armies built to control rather than protect, and rulers who answered to outside powers rather than to citizens. Foreign powers carry real historical responsibility for that, and some still benefit from it.

But Africans were never passive. African rulers, elites, soldiers, movements and ordinary citizens have resisted, adapted, captured and rebuilt these structures, sometimes to free people and sometimes to entrench themselves. Foreign actors have played both roles too. The balance keeps shifting as new partners arrive, continental institutions grow, and a young, connected population pushes back.

Holding these truths together

Colonial and Cold War powers bear real responsibility for building and protecting extractive, unaccountable states, and some foreign governments and companies still profit from them. African leaders and elites bear real responsibility for choices made since independence, including entrenching themselves and capturing the state. And millions of Africans, often alongside foreign allies, have challenged these systems and won real change. Blaming only one actor hides how the system actually works, and hides the power each actor still has to change it.

Who does the Power Stack really serve today?

Because so many actors built it over so long, the system has no single official purpose. But you can judge it by what it reliably produces today. Here are three common answers, and how well each holds up.

Answer 1

To keep the leader in power

PARTLY TRUE

Elections, courts, the army and state money are arranged around the ruler's survival. But rulers do fall, through coups, deaths and the occasional lost election, and the system usually carries on without them.

Answer 2

To serve foreign interests

PARTLY TRUE

Foreign powers get minerals, security cooperation, migration control and diplomatic support. But they compete with each other, and African governments play them off against one another, so no single foreign power controls the outcome.

Answer 3

To serve every actor's interests

TRUE ONLY FOR THE POWERFUL

Each actor with power, from the ruler and the inner circle to the army, lenders, foreign partners and big companies, gets enough to stay on side. Ordinary people are served mainly when it helps keep the peace.

The best answer

The Power Stack is a bargain among the powerful. It keeps the centre in place by giving every strong actor enough of what it wants, and passes most of the cost to ordinary people through weak public services, debt and lost opportunity. That is why it is so stable, and why real change usually means changing what several actors get, not just who sits at the top.

The tension this creates. Because the system is built to keep the powerful on side, improving public welfare often means taking something from someone who holds power: rents, posts, contracts or protection. That is why reforms that would clearly help millions stall, and why change needs many actors to choose public welfare at once.

Everyone is part of it. Whether you are a minister, a soldier, a doctor, a trader, a student or a visitor from the diaspora, your work and choices either reinforce that bargain or push against it. This guide helps you see which.

Part 9 · Money and power

What you earn vs. how close you are to power

Every career path plotted by typical annual earnings (vertical, log scale) against closeness to power in the country type you picked (horizontal). Lines show the typical range; markers show its midpoint, with their shape showing the currency you are paid in. All amounts are converted to US dollars. Your choices move your own dot. Where labels would collide, hover over a dot to see its name; click any dot to load that career.

Earnings are indicative ranges in US dollars per year, estimated from typical salaries and incomes for each role. They vary widely by country, seniority and exchange rate, and are meant for comparison, not as data.

Part 10 · Questions people often ask

Common questions, answered through the Power Stack

Short answers to questions people often ask about Africa's politics, each linked to the part of the system that explains it.

Model limits. This is a general picture built from patterns that repeat across countries. Africa has 54 states with very different systems, and most countries mix features of several country types; pick the closest. Country examples are indicative and change as transitions happen. Labels such as "co-opted opposition" describe a documented pattern in political science; the diagram does not claim any specific party is fake. The closeness-to-power score is a judgement scale for reflection, not a measurement. Nothing here is legal or financial advice.
